title: Resilience Over Time

learn.summary: Resilience is not a trait you have but a system you run: knowing your baseline, catching drift early, and having rehearsed responses ready. Relapse-prevention research (Marlatt) shows setbacks follow patterns — identifiable triggers, early warning signs, and a critical window where small corrections work. The people who stay well are rarely the ones who never dip; they are the ones who notice dips at 20% instead of 80%.

do: Write a half-page 'wellness baseline' today: what your sleep, mood, socializing, and habits look like when you are doing well. This is your reference reading.

children.title: Self-Monitoring

learn.summary: You cannot course-correct what you do not measure, and memory is a terrible instrument — peak-end bias means you recall dramatic moments, not trends. A weekly 2-minute review (mood average, sleep, connection, exercise, one line of notes) outperforms daily obsessing, which can tip into symptom-scanning. The goal is trend detection, not surveillance of every feeling.

do: Set a recurring Sunday reminder and run a 2-minute weekly review (mood 1–10, sleep, connection, movement, one sentence) for four weeks.

children.title: Early Warning Signs

learn.summary: Everyone's slide has a personal signature — common early markers include canceling plans, sleep drift, skipped meals or workouts, doomscrolling spikes, irritability, and letting small admin pile up. Relapse-prevention protocols have patients write these down while well, plus matched if-then responses, because judgment is worst exactly when the signs appear. Marlatt also named the 'abstinence violation effect': one slip becomes a collapse only when interpreted as total failure.

do: List your five personal early-warning signs and write one if-then response for each ('If I cancel plans twice in a week, then I tell X and book one walk with a friend').

children.title: Journaling

learn.summary: James Pennebaker's expressive-writing paradigm — 15–20 minutes writing about a stressor for 3–4 consecutive days — produced measurable improvements in health and mood across dozens of trials; the mechanism seems to be turning inchoate distress into structured narrative. Gratitude journaling (Emmons) is a different tool with different effects: three specific good things, a few times weekly, beats daily rote lists. Caution: journaling that circles the same grievance nightly is rumination with a pen.

do: Run the Pennebaker protocol once: 15 minutes of unfiltered writing about one stressful thing, four days in a row, then decide if it earned a place in your toolkit.
